solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing; clues and answers read from cryptics.georgeho.org (ODbL)'s copy of the post

clue.text: Fringe, associated with Mile in Edinburgh, always havoc

parts.note: in Scots, 'ay' (or 'aye') means always or ever
a hem is the edge or fringe of a garment

explanation.surface: A tourist note about the Edinburgh Fringe festival and the Royal Mile, where chaos always reigns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fringe' and 'Edinburgh' together suggest the festival, but Fringe is simply a hem and Edinburgh only flags a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both words mean wild disorder and destruction.

clue.text: Advert contracted at great expense. But what are they principally saying?

parts.note: advert shortened gives ad

indicators.note: principally points at the leading letter of each of the three words that follow advert

explanation.surface: An advert bought at huge cost, followed by a jibe asking what such ads really tell us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'principally' takes the first letters of 'at great expense', giving AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a saying is a proverb or maxim, a traditional piece of wisdom.

clue.text: Resilience Dick, in first half, shows in tackle

indicators.note: shows in means the first-half piece appears inside the gear word

parts.note: tackle is equipment or gear, as is harness for a horse

indicators.note: first half asks for just the opening two of the four letters of the name Dick

explanation.surface: A rugby report: Dick, playing in the first half, proved tough in the tackle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tackle' reads as a rugby challenge but means gear, as in horse tack; 'first half' keeps the opening two letters of Dick.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: toughness and resilience are both the capacity to withstand hardship.

clue.text: Courage brewer making Mike take over King's Head

indicators.note: take over means the M replaces that letter in the brewer word

parts.note: a kettle brews tea, so it is a brewer in a cryptic sense

indicators.note: Head picks the first letter of the word King's

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Business news: the brewer Courage gets Mike to take over the King's Head pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Courage is a real British brewery and the King's Head a typical pub name, so the surface is all beer; the brewer is really a KETTLE, whose K becomes M.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: mettle is spirit and pluck, the same quality as courage.

clue.text: Be more adventurous, eg knocking back one of Mr Kipling's, tucking into porky pie …

indicators.note: knocking back means the two letters of eg are drunk down in reverse order
tucking into means the poem's title goes inside the word for a fib

parts.note: porky pie is rhyming slang for a lie, a tall story or tale
If- is one of Rudyard Kipling's best-known poems

explanation.surface: Someone knocking back a Mr Kipling cake while stuffing themselves with pork pie is told to find more excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Kipling is a British cake brand, so the surface is all snacks; here it is the poet. Porky pie is Cockney rhyming slang for a lie; 'knocking back' reverses EG and 'tucking into' puts IF into TALE.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: the phrase is a scornful order to stop being dull and do something exciting.

clue.text: Movie featuring GI and the victory over Germany?

indicators.note: over means the victory sits on top of the letter for Germany in this down entry

parts.note: G followed by I, and I is the Roman numeral one, so the two letters give G plus one
with can mean and, as in fish with chips
a victory is a win
D is the international vehicle code for Germany

explanation.surface: A war film about an American GI and the Allied defeat of Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to a Second World War film; the answer is set in the American Civil War. GI must be split into G and I, with I read as the numeral one.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is the famous 1939 Hollywood epic of the American South.

clue.text: Smart hen circles, in US, refuse men

indicators.note: circles suggests the letters of smart hen going round and round into a new order

explanation.surface: A clever hen running rings round some American bin collectors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circles' rearranges SMART HEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Regional term: American usage for the men who collect household rubbish.

clue.text: Owner of estate car ultimately limited by turning circle

indicators.note: limited by means the car's final letter is enclosed by the turned circle
turning means the word for the circular face is read backwards

parts.note: a dial is a circular face, as on a clock or phone

indicators.note: ultimately picks the final letter of the word car

explanation.surface: An estate car driven round a limited turning circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'estate car' is a single phrase in the surface but splits here: 'Owner of estate' is the definition and car gives its last letter R. 'turning' reverses DIAL to LAID.
explanation.definitionFit: Scottish term: a laird owns a landed estate in Scotland.

clue.text: Fellow phoned Lisa, exercising informal language

parts.note: rang means telephoned

indicators.note: exercising suggests Lisa's letters being worked and moved about into a new order

explanation.surface: A man phoned Lisa while she was working out, chatting casually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exercising' rearranges LISA into LAIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a casual hybrid of French sprinkled with English words, not a formal tongue.

clue.text: Contrarily, design includes gold on bronze liner

indicators.note: includes means the reversed intention word holds the other letters inside
Contrarily means the word for intention is turned the other way

parts.note: a design is an aim or intention
Au is the chemical symbol for gold
re means on or about, as in a letter heading
tan is a bronze colour

explanation.surface: An awkward interior design with gold set on bronze, as on an ornate ocean liner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contrarily' turns AIM into MIA, which 'includes' AU, RE and TAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a famous Cunard ocean liner, sister ship to the Lusitania.

clue.text: Terrible ruler — only 1/3 of values written in inches

indicators.note: written in means those letters are placed within the abbreviation

parts.note: in is the abbreviation for inches

indicators.note: only 1/3 of takes the opening third, two letters of six, of the word values

explanation.surface: A dreadful ruler on which only a third of the markings are written in inches.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'ruler' is a monarch, not a measuring stick: Ivan the Terrible of Russia.
explanation.definitionFit: Epithet: the first tsar of Russia is remembered as Ivan the Terrible.

clue.text: Autographed drawing missing — George, Bobby and another Man Utd icon?

indicators.note: missing means a letter is dropped from the reversed word
drawing is read as drawing back, so the word for autographed is pulled the other way

parts.note: autographed means signed
G is the initial for George
a bobby is a policeman, and the police are the law

explanation.surface: A signed drawing has gone missing, of George Best, Bobby Charlton and one more Manchester United legend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drawing' reverses SIGNED to DENGIS; 'missing' George takes out G. George and Bobby look like Best and Charlton, but give G and LAW.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the Scottish striker was United's star alongside Best and Charlton in the 1960s.

clue.text: Tried injecting female bit of glamour into house

indicators.note: into means the name and letter are injected inside the house abbreviation

parts.note: Ada is a female name

indicators.note: bit of takes just the opening letter of glamour

explanation.surface: Someone attempted to bring a touch of feminine glamour into their home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'injecting' and 'into' both signal the insertion; 'bit of' gives the first letter of glamour.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to have a go is to make an attempt, so the phrase means tried.

clue.text: Out of work, but regularly indulge

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of indulge, starting with the first

explanation.surface: Unemployed, yet still treating yourself now and then.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: someone without a job is idle, not working.

clue.text: Fling mashed potato, say, around pan edge in infancy

indicators.note: around means the dance word wraps the other letters

parts.note: the Mashed Potato was a 1960s dance craze
pan- is the Greek prefix for all

indicators.note: edge picks the leading letter of infancy

explanation.surface: A toddler throwing mashed potato across the edge of a pan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fling' looks like a verb about hurling food but is a noun, a brief affair. 'mashed potato' is the dance; pan- (Greek 'all') gives ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a fling is a casual romantic affair, which is what a dalliance is.

clue.text: Country sadly hadn't attracted employment after revolution

indicators.note: attracted means the rearranged letters draw the reversed word in among them
sadly suggests hadn't being broken up into a new arrangement
after revolution means the word for employment is turned round

parts.note: employment means use

explanation.surface: After the revolution the country unfortunately failed to bring in jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges the letters of hadn't, 'after revolution' turns the employment word round, and 'attracted' draws it into the middle of the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the African nation is often written with the article.

clue.text: Single male penetrates novel in Dutch

indicators.note: penetrates means the pronoun goes inside the rearranged letters
novel as an adjective means new, so the letters of in Dutch take a new order

parts.note: he is a male pronoun

explanation.surface: A lone man breaks into a novel written in Dutch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' rearranges IN DUTCH, and HE goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang sense: someone no longer married or attached is free and on their own.

clue.text: Stretch Roller one brought into school, reversing for example

indicators.note: brought into means those letters are placed inside the group word

parts.note: a pod is a school of whales or dolphins
RR stands for Rolls-Royce, whose car is a Roller
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: reversing means the two letters are turned round

explanation.surface: A Rolls-Royce brought into a school and reversing, perhaps on a long drive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roller' is British slang for a Rolls-Royce. 'Stretch' is prison time, and PORRIDGE is British slang for a jail sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang: both mean a term served in prison.

clue.text: Openness of parent: Son's algebra is going backwards!

indicators.note: going backwards says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A parent exclaiming that their son's maths is getting worse.
explanation.walkthrough: No word marks the hiding; the answer is concealed backwards across parent, Son's and algebra.
explanation.definitionFit: Loanword: the Soviet policy of transparency under Gorbachev, now a general term for openness.

clue.text: What food is like in hospitals?

definitions.text: What food is like in hospitals?

indicators.note: in means the comparison word sits between the two hospital letters

parts.note: H is the map abbreviation for hospital, so two hospitals give two H's
as means like

explanation.surface: A gripe about the quality of hospital meals.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: AS inside H and H, and a jibe that hospital food is a mess.
explanation.definitionFit: Double sense: hash is a dish of chopped leftovers and also a mess, as in making a hash of it.

clue.text: Harmonious pub keeps emptying Surrey college

indicators.note: keeps means the pub word holds the letters inside

parts.note: an inn is a pub

indicators.note: emptying removes everything but the outer letters of Surrey

explanation.surface: A local pub that keeps clearing out students from a Surrey college.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is an English county; 'emptying' removes its middle letters, leaving just the outside pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: being in sync means moving or working together in harmony.

clue.text: Group of cats piddling — sidestep left and right

indicators.note: sidestep means one L is avoided, dropped from the word for trivial

parts.note: piddling means trivial or little

explanation.surface: Cats peeing about, so you have to step around them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'piddling' looks like urination but means small; 'sidestep' drops one L from LITTLE and R is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Collective noun: a set of kittens born together is so called.

clue.text: Swimmer, outside of the craft, surfaced

indicators.note: outside of keeps only the end letters of the word the
surfaced means the skill word rises, read upwards in this down entry

parts.note: art is a craft or skill

explanation.surface: A diver comes up beside the boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'craft' looks like a boat but means ART, which 'surfaced' turns upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a small, brightly coloured tropical aquarium fish.

clue.text: Boffin, first in engineering, occupying piano? No way

indicators.note: first in takes the opening letter of engineering

parts.note: occupying means in, as in being in a house

indicators.note: No means the following word is taken away

parts.note: a Steinway is a famous make of piano
taken as written

explanation.surface: A scientist, first in his engineering class, sits at the piano: no chance.
explanation.walkthrough: Steinway is a piano brand; 'No way' removes WAY, leaving STEIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the physicist's name stands for a genius; boffin is British slang for a scientist.

clue.text: Fashionista, releasing latest in sex appeal, displays ass

indicators.note: in means the shortened name goes inside the slang word

parts.note: it is old slang for sex appeal

indicators.note: releasing latest drops the final letter of the fashion name

parts.note: Dior is a famous fashion house

explanation.surface: A fashion figure loses their sex appeal and makes a fool of themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' meaning sex appeal comes from the 1920s 'It girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an ass is a fool or simpleton.

clue.text: Create pullover? By end of week, one could get attached to it

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of week

parts.words: one could get attached to it
parts.note: a nit, a louse egg, is glued firmly to a hair, so it is one thing that could get attached

explanation.surface: A plan to make a jumper by the weekend, something you could grow fond of.
explanation.walkthrough: A pullover (British jumper) is made with needles and wool. The second half is a cryptic hint for NIT, the louse egg that clings to hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a pullover is a woollen garment, made by looping yarn with needles.

clue.text: Outsiders to supply tea in India, arranging connecting train

indicators.note: in means those letters sit within the rearranged country
arranging puts the letters of India into a new order
Outsiders to keeps only the end letters of supply

parts.note: cha is a slang word for tea

explanation.surface: Arranging a supply of tea in India and a train connection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranging' rearranges INDIA into DAI...IN; SY (the ends of supply) and CHA go 'in' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a string of flowers linked stem to stem, a connected chain or train.

clue.text: The 2 contrived to be successful

indicators.note: contrived suggests the letters being forced into a new arrangement

parts.note: 2 points to the answer of clue 2 down, a saying

explanation.surface: A well-worn saying, artificially set up, about how to succeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contrived' rearranges THE plus the 2-down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to get on or advance in life or career.

clue.text: Low grades gained by musical students

indicators.note: gained by means the grades are taken inside the show's title

parts.note: Cats is Andrew Lloyd Webber's musical
D and E are low exam grades

explanation.surface: Music students getting poor marks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'musical' is the show CATS, not an adjective describing the students.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: cadets are trainees, especially in the forces or police.
